fetched_contents.text: Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) | NESDIS The Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) is a single-channel, near-infrared optical detector on the GOES-R Series satellites. It is the first instrument of its kind to continuously map lightning from geostationary orbit, detecting quick flashes in the atmosphere that indicate in-cloud, cloud-to-cloud, and cloud-to-ground strikes. Because of its vantage point, GLM can monitor large areas over time, even over oceans and regions with limited radar coverage. GLM also offers insights beyond the presence of a lightning strike, revealing the extent of lightning flashes and the distance they travel. Its data helps produce a long-term database to track lightning activity over decades, which can give insight into the Earth-atmosphere electrical balance. Note to screen-readers: This page is using an IFrame for the content-area, and you screen reader may not be abel to see it on this website. For screen-reading purposes, please go directly to the IFrame's target page by going to https://www.youtube.com/embed/7oOU3lsQyQk?si=Y1_41qVk2B701IGH?rel=1. Tracking Lightning to Improve Safety and Forecasting Rapid increases in lightning activity can indicate that a thunderstorm is intensifying. Since storms can intensify very quickly, it’s important to get that data as fast as possible. While radar updates roughly every 5 minutes, the lightning mapper updates every 20-60 seconds, making it a valuable tool in forecasting severe weather. Lightning activity detected by the GLM alerts forecasters to possible tornadoes, large hail, damaging winds, and even hurricane intensification before severe weather strikes.It’s also used to inform lightning hazard warnings, estimate precipitation, identify lightning flashes most likely to ignite wildfires, and mitigate aviation hazards. This technology is especially beneficial in rural or mountainous areas, as well as over open oceans, where other data resources such as radar and surface observations may be limited. Severe Thunderstorm and Tornado Warnings Storms that go on to produce damaging winds, hail, and even tornadoes often show a significant jump in lightning activity. With the GLM, the increase in lightning can be seen minutes before radar detects signs of severe weather. Combined with radar, other satellite data, and surface observations, total lightning data from the GLM can help get severe thunderstorm and tornado warnings out sooner and reduce false alarms. GOES-16 captured lightning illuminating the sky across the South as severe thunderstorms charged eastward. Credit: NOAA Precipitation Estimates Lightning activity is closely tied to strong convection currents, such as updrafts– the warm, moist rising air that fuels storms. The more lightning detected usually means the stronger the storm and increasing potential for heavy rain or hail is likely. By combining GLM lightning data with radar and satellite images, meteorologists can put together faster and more accurate precipitation forecasts. Hurricane Forecasting For hurricanes, the GLM reveals lightning patterns within the storm that reveal changes in structure and intensity. These insights help forecasters understand how a storm is evolving, which leads to more accurate predictions for where the storm will track and how strong it will be. Hurricane Helene. Credit: CSU/CIRA & NOAA Improving Lightning Safety Lightning can strike ground as far as 100 miles from a thunderstorm, so knowing its prevalence and spatial distribution helps forecasters warn the public when it’s unsafe. This is vital during outdoor activities, such as fishing, enjoying the beach, boating, camping, playing soccer, mowing the lawn, and farming. Watersports are especially risky. For example, lightning over the ocean is especially hazardous since boats travel far from shelter, a boat’s engine makes it more difficult to hear thunder, and it takes longer to find a safe location. The GLM data can be minutes ahead of radar, giving the public more time to get out of harm's way, whether that’s on the water or on land. It’s also free, publicly available, and easy to interpret, allowing those responsible for others in outdoor activities to make quick, informed lightning safety decisions. Aviation and Airport Weather Warnings To protect ground crews at airports, alerts typically are issued when lightning strikes within five miles of the airport, and operations are halted when it strikes within three miles. The GLM provides tremendous benefit for these situations, helping to alert airport operators of potential danger. The airline industry also benefits from using lightning mapping data to reduce weather-related costs. The lightning data contributes to cost savings through reduced fuel use and fewer delays and diversions. GLM data support the efficiency of both ramp operations and airplanes in the sky, on approach, and on the taxiway. For pilots, GLM data warns of dangerous thunderstorms before and during flight, allowing them to plan routes to avoid lightning strikes to their aircraft and turbulence from severe weather. This is especially valuable when there are storms over the open ocean because there are fewer sources of storm detection. Wildfire Response Lightning strikes ignite more than half of the acreage burned by wildfires in the U.S., routinely sparking the costliest and deadliest fire complexes. Many of these fires begin in remote areas and go undetected for hours after they start. That’s because lightning can strike in less populated areas where ground detection sources are limited and response resources have to be brought in, delaying both detection and firefighting efforts. GLM is uniquely able to monitor vast areas and identify lightning flashes most likely to ignite fires. This information can help emergency personnel respond sooner, reducing property damage and firefighting costs and potentially saving lives. fetched_contents.text: ISS: LIS (Lightning Imaging Sensor) EO | Atmosphere | NASA | Mission complete | The International Space Station Lightning Imaging Sensor mission (ISS:LIS), was developed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and Marshall Space Flight Centre (MSFC), it was originally flown on TRMM (Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission) but now is a hosted payload on a SpaceX vehicle. The mission monitors the quantity, rate, and radiant energy of Earth’s lightning. It has increased awareness of thunderstorms and geophysical hazards, improving society’s ability to respond to them, by monitoring regions like oceans. It was launched on 19 February 2017 and the current mission status is operational. Quick facts Overview Mission type EO Agency NASA Mission status Mission complete Launch date 19 Feb 2017 End of life date 30 Oct 2023 Measurement domain Atmosphere Measurement category Lightning Detection Measurement detailed Total lightning density Instruments LIS Instrument type Lightning sensors CEOS EO Handbook See ISS: LIS (Lightning Imaging Sensor) summary Related Resources Summary Mission Capabilities ISS:LIS carries LIS (Lightning Image Sensor). LIS primarily operates as a transient event detector for ISS and is made up of a combination of optical and electrical elements. It is a small solid-state optical imager that detects lightning from a low earth orbit, measuring the time and radiant energy of an occurrence. LIS uses the ISS’s low rate telemetry channel to provide real time lightning data. Performance Specifications ISS:LIS has a spatial resolution of 4km with the maximum latitude coverage of about ±54.33º. It has a swath width of about 550 km as well as a revisit time of about 4 days (as this suits the swath width of the LIS ) , as determined by the orbit of the ISS.. A key point of development for LIS was location accuracy which is within one pixel. As LIS is hosted on the ISS, it follows an inclined, non-sun-synchronous orbit at an altitude of 405km and an inclination of 51° Space and Hardware Components In order to focus the image on a tiny, high-speed 128 x 128 charge-coupled device(CCD) focal plane, the design utilises an expanded optics which covers a broad field-of-view and a narrow-band interference filter that is concentrated on the strong oxygen emission line (i.e., the oxygen multiplet at OI (Oxygen Iodine) line at 777.4 nm) in the lightning spectrum. In 2001,LIS on the TRMM and another detector; the Optical Transient Detector (OTD), on the commercial OrbView-1 satellite, created the first global map of lightning activity. The ISS:LIS,the TRMM’s LIS and the OTD are continuously adding to the records that contributed to the map created in January 2021. ISS Utilization: LIS (Lightning Imaging Sensor) on STP-H5's investigations of DoD Launch Mission Status Instrument Description Ground Segment References LIS, flown on the TRMM (Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission) of NASA (launch Nov. 27, 1997), was designed and developed at NASA/MSFC, the UAH (University of Alabama in Huntsville), and their partners. Hugh Christian of UAH is the PI (Principal Investigator) of LIS. After more than 17 years on orbit, the instrument has demonstrated successfully space-based lightning observations as an effective remote sensing tool for Earth science research and applications. In April 2013, a space-qualified LIS built as the flight spare for TRMM, was selected for flight as a science mission on the International Space Station. The ISS-LIS will be flown as a hosted payload on the DoD STP-H5’s investigations mission, which is scheduled for launch in 2017 aboard a SpaceX launch vehicle for a 2-4 year or longer mission. 1) The LIS measures the amount, rate, and radiant energy of total lightning over the Earth. More specifically, it measures lightning during both day and night, with storm scale resolution (~4 km), millisecond timing, and high, uniform detection efficiency, without any land-ocean bias. Lightning is a direct and most impressive response to intense atmospheric convection. It has been found that lightning measured by LIS can be quantitatively related to thunderstorm and other geophysical processes. Therefore, the ISS -LIS lightning observations will continue to provide important gap-filling inputs to pressing Earth system science issues across a broad range of disciplines, including weather, climate, atmospheric chemistry, and lightning physics. 2) Background NASA’s first spaceborne lightning sensor, called OTD ( Optical Transient Detector), was launched aboard the MicroLab-1 satellite in 1995 from Vandenberg Air Force Base. The primary mission of the OTD instrument was to improve the understanding of thunderstorm distributions, cloud processes, and storm variability by detecting lightning activity over large areas of the Earth’s surface. The concept for this instrument was developed at MSFC in the 1980s, and was selected for development as part of NASA’s Earth Observing System (EOS). 3) Prior to 1995, spaceborne lightning observations had been severely limited by one or more problems, including low or unknown detection efficiency, poor spatial and temporal resolution, a limited number or brief periods of observations, and an inability to measure lightning during the daytime, leading to incomplete sampling over the diurnal cycle. The launch of OTD ushered in a new era of spaceborne lightning detection, being specifically designed to address the deficiencies of available ground-based, in situ, and space-based lightning measurements. In particular, it provided—for the first time—highly detailed and accurate statistics of the geographical distribution of lightning frequency, worldwide. The OTD was positioned in a near-circular orbit at an altitude of 740 km , at a 70º inclination. This orbit provided observations of lightning activity over most regions of the world where lightning is generated (coverage between 75º N and S latitude). Satellite systems compare with ground-based systems in coverage and capability because ground-based systems are inherently limited by the sparse and uneven distribution of detection networks. The evidence explicitly states that “ground-based total lightning detection spatial coverage is restricted to the limited number and sparse distribution of networks capable of detecting total lightning” [N3-F3]. This means coverage is constrained by the number and placement of sensors, which can leave large areas, especially over oceans or remote regions, undersampled. Ground-based systems still outperform satellites in some respects: they can provide higher-resolution, more localized lightning characteristics because they detect VHF emissions and can resolve lightning sources in three dimensions [N3-F3]. They are also better at identifying the exact spatial and temporal structure of individual lightning flashes, which matters for detailed storm analysis and early warnings [N3-F3].

Satellite systems overcome those limitations by using a much broader vantage point. The GLM, for example, is described as a satellite-based instrument that can monitor large areas over time, even over oceans and regions with limited radar coverage [N1-F1]. LIS is also noted as being able to detect lightning from low-Earth orbit and provide global sampling, with LIS improving detection efficiency and spatial resolution because of its lower orbit altitude [N2-F2]. The historical context in the provided material shows that early spaceborne sensors were designed to address the deficiencies of ground-based and in situ measurements, especially low or unknown detection efficiency, poor spatial and temporal resolution, and the inability to measure lightning during the daytime [N2-F2]. The result is a system that can observe lightning over much larger regions, including remote areas and the ocean, where ground networks are sparse or absent [N1-F1].

The tradeoffs are still important. Ground-based systems remain superior for high-resolution, three-dimensional lightning characterization and for detecting lightning flashes that satellites might miss due to cloud shielding or geometry [N3-F3]. Satellites, by contrast, excel at global and large-area coverage, continuous monitoring, and detecting lightning over ocean and remote regions [N1-F1]. The evidence also implies that satellites can reduce missing events in regions where ground networks are sparse, but they may still suffer from detection efficiency tradeoffs, such as lower efficiency at night or in certain cloudy conditions [N2-F2]. In short, satellites improve coverage and detection over broad regions, while ground-based systems remain better at detailed, localized lightning detection [N3-F3][N1-F1][N2-F2].

## How satellite-based lightning sensors have improved lightning monitoring over time

Satellite-based lightning sensors have improved lightning monitoring in two major ways: **spatial coverage** and **detection capability**. Over time, satellite systems have moved from early low-Earth-orbiting sensors toward continuous global monitoring, while sensor design, algorithmic processing, and data fusion have steadily improved detection accuracy, reduced false alarms, and minimized missing events [N1-R3][N1-R1][N2-F2][N2-R5][N4-F4][N6-R1].

### 1) Expanded spatial coverage over time

The progression of satellite missions shows a clear expansion in global coverage. The earliest direct evidence points to the **Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS)** and the earlier **Optical Transient Detector (OTD)**, with LIS described as a low-Earth-orbiting sensor designed to detect lightning from space [N1-R3][N2-F2]. LIS was also noted as improving detection efficiency and spatial resolution because of its lower orbit altitude [N2-F2]. Later, the **Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM)** became a major leap forward, representing a geostationary satellite with a single-channel near-infrared optical detector that continuously maps lightning from geostationary orbit [N1-R2][N1-F1]. This shift from low-Earth orbit to geostationary orbit dramatically broadened the detectable area.

Orbital altitude and instrument geometry affect detectable regions in important ways. LIS, at a lower orbit, achieved better spatial resolution than earlier systems, with evidence stating that LIS’s increased sensitivity and lower orbit altitude improved spatial resolution to 4 km [N2-F2]. GLM, in contrast, operates in geostationary orbit, giving it a much larger field of view and the ability to monitor large areas continuously over the Americas and adjacent ocean regions [N1-F1]. GLM is also described as especially beneficial in **rural or mountainous areas** and **over open oceans**, where other data resources such as radar and surface observations may be limited [N1-F1]. LIS, by comparison, can observe lightning over much of the globe, including remote oceanic areas [N2-F2].

The evidence also indicates that LIS had a maximum latitude coverage of about ±54.33º and a swath width of about 550 km, but its revisit time was about 4 days [N2-F2]. GLM, by contrast, has continuous coverage because it is geostationary, which means it can monitor large regions without long revisit gaps [N1-F1]. This means that satellite coverage has improved not only in scale but also in continuity over time.

Regions or environments that have improved the most in coverage include **oceans, remote areas, and regions with limited radar coverage**. The evidence explicitly states that GLM is especially useful over oceans and where radar and surface observations are sparse [N1-F1]. LIS is also noted as helping monitor regions like oceans [N2-F2]. The case-study evidence further suggests that regional coverage has improved in **western North America, Europe, Eastern Asia, Australia, Africa, and southern South America** [N5-R5]. Taken together, satellite-based monitoring has moved from sparse global sampling to much broader, more continuous coverage, especially where ground networks are sparse or absent [N1-R3][N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-R5].

### 2) Improved detection capabilities over time

Detection capabilities have improved through better sensor design, more accurate algorithms, and improved data processing. LIS was specifically developed to address deficiencies in earlier spaceborne measurements, including low or unknown detection efficiency, poor spatial and temporal resolution, and inability to measure lightning during the daytime [N2-F2]. LIS’s increased sensitivity and lower orbit altitude improved spatial resolution to 4 km [N2-F2]. GLM, as a geostationary sensor, is described as having “near-uniform spatial resolution” and broader, continuous coverage capability, which likely improves detection by reducing missing events in large regions [N2-R5][N1-F1]. These sensor design changes reflect a direct improvement in detection accuracy: LIS improved detection efficiency and resolution, while GLM improved coverage and continuity [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Algorithm changes have also improved detection accuracy. The evidence points to **data fusion** and **machine learning** as important advances. For example, LIS/OTD built a global lightning record by combining LIS, TRMM LIS, and OTD, which implies that algorithmic fusion across multiple sensors enhances completeness [N2-F2]. More recently, deep learning has been used for lightning prediction and lightning nowcasting, including semantic segmentation networks for cloud-to-ground lightning and multi-hazard models that predict lightning, hail, and heavy precipitation [N4-R2][N4-R3]. This indicates that algorithms are moving from simple detection rules to more sophisticated models that can better capture lightning dynamics and reduce false alarms [N4-F4]. The lightning prediction survey also notes that deep learning can improve accuracy and efficiency, and that it is increasingly used for spatio-temporal lightning prediction [N4-F4].

Improved data processing reduces missing events and noise. The evidence shows that GLM data can be used with radar, satellite data, and surface observations to improve severe weather warnings and reduce false alarms [N1-F1]. LIS and OTD built a global record by combining data from multiple sensors, suggesting that data fusion reduces gaps and missing events [N2-F2]. The LIS validation plan explicitly addresses detection efficiency and false alarms, which is central to reducing missing events and noise [N6-R1]. The lightning prediction survey also emphasizes that data-driven methods can improve accuracy by capturing intricate data patterns, which implies better noise reduction and event identification [N4-F4]. Taken together, the evidence indicates that detection capabilities have improved through higher-sensitivity sensors, better algorithms, and more sophisticated data processing that together reduce false alarms, improve detection efficiency, and decrease missing lightning events [N2-F2][N1-F1][N4-F4][N6-R1].

### 3) Comparison with ground-based systems

Satellite systems compare with ground-based systems in coverage and capability because ground-based systems are inherently limited by the sparse and uneven distribution of detection networks. The evidence explicitly states that “ground-based total lightning detection spatial coverage is restricted to the limited number and sparse distribution of networks capable of detecting total lightning” [N3-F3]. This means coverage is constrained by the number and placement of sensors, which can leave large areas, especially over oceans or remote regions, undersampled. Ground-based systems still outperform satellites in some respects: they can provide higher-resolution, more localized lightning characteristics because they detect VHF emissions and can resolve lightning sources in three dimensions [N3-F3]. They are also better at identifying the exact spatial and temporal structure of individual lightning flashes, which matters for detailed storm analysis and early warnings [N3-F3].

Satellite systems overcome those limitations by using a much broader vantage point. GLM is described as a satellite-based instrument that can monitor large areas over time, even over oceans and regions with limited radar coverage [N1-F1]. LIS is also noted as being able to detect lightning from low-Earth orbit and provide global sampling, with LIS improving detection efficiency and spatial resolution because of its lower orbit altitude [N1-R3][N2-F2]. The historical context in the provided material shows that early spaceborne sensors were designed to address the deficiencies of ground-based and in situ measurements, especially low or unknown detection efficiency, poor spatial and temporal resolution, and the inability to measure lightning during the daytime [N2-F2]. The result is a system that can observe lightning over much larger regions, including remote areas and the ocean, where ground networks are sparse or absent [N1-F1].

The tradeoffs are still important. Ground-based systems remain superior for high-resolution, three-dimensional lightning characterization and for detecting lightning flashes that satellites might miss due to cloud shielding or geometry [N3-F3]. Satellites, by contrast, excel at global and large-area coverage, continuous monitoring, and detecting lightning over ocean and remote regions [N1-F1]. The evidence also implies that satellites can reduce missing events in regions where ground networks are sparse, but they may still suffer from detection efficiency tradeoffs, such as lower efficiency at night or in certain cloudy conditions [N2-F2]. In short, satellites improve coverage and detection over broad regions, while ground-based systems remain better at detailed, localized lightning detection [N3-F3][N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 4) Practical implications for monitoring and operations

Better coverage and detection support weather forecasting and hazard monitoring in several practical ways. First, GLM can detect lightning continuously over large areas and over oceans, which is especially valuable for severe weather forecasting because lightning activity can indicate intensifying thunderstorms before radar detects signs of severe weather [N1-F1]. It can also help produce earlier severe thunderstorm and tornado warnings and reduce false alarms when combined with radar, satellite data, and surface observations [N1-F1]. The evidence emphasizes that lightning is especially useful for detecting, analyzing, and forecasting severe weather, and that it can warn forecasters about possible tornadoes, large hail, damaging winds, and hurricane intensification [N1-F1]. For hazard monitoring, GLM supports lightning hazard warnings, wildfire response, aviation safety, and maritime safety, because lightning can strike far from thunderstorms and is hazardous on the water or in open areas where shelter is limited [N1-F1]. It also helps identify lightning flashes most likely to ignite wildfires, which is important for emergency response and fire mitigation [N1-F1].

Operational constraints still limit satellite lightning systems. One major constraint is the need for **cloud shielding**: the evidence says that lightning is detected from space due to the illumination of the surrounding clouds, implying that clouds can obscure lightning flashes and reduce detection [N3-R1]. GLM’s detection efficiency is also affected by orbital geometry and sensor limitations, as LIS improved detection efficiency and spatial resolution by lowering its orbit, while GLM’s geostationary vantage point gives broad coverage but not the same fine-scale resolution [N1-R3][N2-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence also indicates that satellite systems can miss lightning flashes when ground networks are sparse, and that algorithmic and data-processing challenges remain in reducing missing events and noise [N2-F2][N4-F4]. In short, satellites are powerful for large-area monitoring, but they still struggle with cloud shielding, lower resolution in some conditions, and the need for complementary ground networks to fill gaps.

Remaining gaps in spatial and temporal coverage include regions with limited radar coverage and areas where lightning activity is most intense or where ground networks are sparse. The GLM overview explicitly states that it is especially beneficial in rural or mountainous areas and over open oceans where radar and surface observations may be limited [N1-F1]. LIS is also noted as improving coverage in remote oceanic areas [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also shows that satellite systems still depend on orbital revisit times and sensor geometry to capture lightning: LIS has a 4-day revisit time, while GLM has continuous coverage but not unlimited spatial detail [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The case-study evidence implies that regional coverage has improved in some places, but gaps still exist because lightning monitoring remains uneven, especially in areas where ground networks are not dense enough [N5-R5]. Overall, better coverage and detection improve forecasting and hazard monitoring, but satellites still need to be supplemented by ground systems and improved algorithms to reduce missing events and cloud-related errors [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

### Conclusion

Overall, satellite-based lightning sensors have improved lightning monitoring over time by expanding spatial coverage from early low-Earth-orbiting sensors to continuous global monitoring via geostationary systems, while improving detection capability through better sensor design, more accurate algorithms, and improved data processing [N1-R3][N1-R1][N2-F2][N2-R5][N4-F4][N6-R1]. Satellite systems now provide broad, continuous coverage over oceans and remote areas where ground networks are sparse, but they still face tradeoffs with resolution, cloud shielding, and the need for complementary ground-based observations [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R1]. Ground-based systems remain superior for high-resolution, three-dimensional lightning characterization and detailed storm analysis, while satellites excel at large-area monitoring and early warning [N3-F3][N1-F1]. The result is a more complete, timely, and operationally useful lightning monitoring system that supports weather forecasting, hazard monitoring, and safety decision-making [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R5].

## How satellite-based lightning sensors have improved lightning monitoring over time

Satellite-based lightning sensors have improved lightning monitoring in two major ways: **spatial coverage** and **detection capability**. Over time, satellite systems have moved from early low-Earth-orbiting sensors toward continuous global monitoring, while sensor design, algorithmic processing, and data fusion have steadily improved detection accuracy, reduced false alarms, and minimized missing events [N1-R3][N1-R1][N2-F2][N2-R5][N4-F4][N6-R1].

### 1) Expanded spatial coverage over time

The progression of satellite missions shows a clear expansion in global coverage. The earliest direct evidence points to the **Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS)** and the earlier **Optical Transient Detector (OTD)**, with LIS described as a low-Earth-orbiting sensor designed to detect lightning from space [N1-R3][N2-F2]. LIS was also noted as improving detection efficiency and spatial resolution because of its lower orbit altitude [N2-F2]. Later, the **Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM)** became a major leap forward, representing a geostationary satellite with a single-channel near-infrared optical detector that continuously maps lightning from geostationary orbit [N1-R2][N1-F1]. This shift from low-Earth orbit to geostationary orbit dramatically broadened the detectable area.

Orbital altitude and instrument geometry affect detectable regions in important ways. LIS, at a lower orbit, achieved better spatial resolution than earlier systems, with evidence stating that LIS’s increased sensitivity and lower orbit altitude improved spatial resolution to 4 km [N2-F2]. GLM, in contrast, operates in geostationary orbit, giving it a much larger field of view and the ability to monitor large areas continuously over the Americas and adjacent ocean regions [N1-F1]. GLM is also described as especially beneficial in **rural or mountainous areas** and **over open oceans**, where other data resources such as radar and surface observations may be limited [N1-F1]. LIS, by comparison, can observe lightning over much of the globe, including remote oceanic areas [N2-F2].

The evidence also indicates that LIS had a maximum latitude coverage of about ±54.33º and a swath width of about 550 km, but its revisit time was about 4 days [N2-F2]. GLM, by contrast, has continuous coverage because it is geostationary, which means it can monitor large regions without long revisit gaps [N1-F1]. This means that satellite coverage has improved not only in scale but also in continuity over time.

Regions or environments that have improved the most in coverage include **oceans, remote areas, and regions with limited radar coverage**. The evidence explicitly states that GLM is especially useful over oceans and where radar and surface observations are sparse [N1-F1]. LIS is also noted as helping monitor regions like oceans [N2-F2]. The case-study evidence further suggests that regional coverage has improved in **western North America, Europe, Eastern Asia, Australia, Africa, and southern South America** [N5-R5]. Taken together, satellite-based monitoring has moved from sparse global sampling to much broader, more continuous coverage, especially where ground networks are sparse or absent [N1-R3][N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-R5].

### 2) Improved detection capabilities over time

Detection capabilities have improved through better sensor design, more accurate algorithms, and improved data processing. LIS was specifically developed to address deficiencies in earlier spaceborne measurements, including low or unknown detection efficiency, poor spatial and temporal resolution, and inability to measure lightning during the daytime [N2-F2]. LIS’s increased sensitivity and lower orbit altitude improved spatial resolution to 4 km [N2-F2]. GLM, as a geostationary sensor, is described as having “near-uniform spatial resolution” and broader, continuous coverage capability, which likely improves detection by reducing missing events in large regions [N2-R5][N1-F1]. These sensor design changes reflect a direct improvement in detection accuracy: LIS improved detection efficiency and resolution, while GLM improved coverage and continuity [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Algorithm changes have also improved detection accuracy. The evidence points to **data fusion** and **machine learning** as important advances. For example, LIS/OTD built a global lightning record by combining LIS, TRMM LIS, and OTD, which implies that algorithmic fusion across multiple sensors enhances completeness [N2-F2]. More recently, deep learning has been used for lightning prediction and lightning nowcasting, including semantic segmentation networks for cloud-to-ground lightning and multi-hazard models that predict lightning, hail, and heavy precipitation [N4-R2][N4-R3]. This indicates that algorithms are moving from simple detection rules to more sophisticated models that can better capture lightning dynamics and reduce false alarms [N4-F4]. The lightning prediction survey also notes that deep learning can improve accuracy and efficiency, and that it is increasingly used for spatio-temporal lightning prediction [N4-F4].

Improved data processing reduces missing events and noise. The evidence shows that GLM data can be used with radar, satellite data, and surface observations to improve severe weather warnings and reduce false alarms [N1-F1]. LIS and OTD built a global record by combining data from multiple sensors, suggesting that data fusion reduces gaps and missing events [N2-F2]. The LIS validation plan explicitly addresses detection efficiency and false alarms, which is central to reducing missing events and noise [N6-R1]. The lightning prediction survey also emphasizes that data-driven methods can improve accuracy by capturing intricate data patterns, which implies better noise reduction and event identification [N4-F4]. Taken together, the evidence indicates that detection capabilities have improved through higher-sensitivity sensors, better algorithms, and more sophisticated data processing that together reduce false alarms, improve detection efficiency, and decrease missing lightning events [N2-F2][N1-F1][N4-F4][N6-R1].

### 3) Comparison with ground-based systems

Satellite systems compare with ground-based systems in coverage and capability because ground-based systems are inherently limited by the sparse and uneven distribution of detection networks. The evidence explicitly states that “ground-based total lightning detection spatial coverage is restricted to the limited number and sparse distribution of networks capable of detecting total lightning” [N3-F3]. This means coverage is constrained by the number and placement of sensors, which can leave large areas, especially over oceans or remote regions, undersampled. Ground-based systems still outperform satellites in some respects: they can provide higher-resolution, more localized lightning characteristics because they detect VHF emissions and can resolve lightning sources in three dimensions [N3-F3]. They are also better at identifying the exact spatial and temporal structure of individual lightning flashes, which matters for detailed storm analysis and early warnings [N3-F3].

Satellite systems overcome those limitations by using a much broader vantage point. GLM is described as a satellite-based instrument that can monitor large areas over time, even over oceans and regions with limited radar coverage [N1-F1]. LIS is also noted as being able to detect lightning from low-Earth orbit and provide global sampling, with LIS improving detection efficiency and spatial resolution because of its lower orbit altitude [N1-R3][N2-F2]. The historical context in the provided material shows that early spaceborne sensors were designed to address the deficiencies of ground-based and in situ measurements, especially low or unknown detection efficiency, poor spatial and temporal resolution, and the inability to measure lightning during the daytime [N2-F2]. The result is a system that can observe lightning over much larger regions, including remote areas and the ocean, where ground networks are sparse or absent [N1-F1].

The tradeoffs are still important. Ground-based systems remain superior for high-resolution, three-dimensional lightning characterization and for detecting lightning flashes that satellites might miss due to cloud shielding or geometry [N3-F3]. Satellites, by contrast, excel at global and large-area coverage, continuous monitoring, and detecting lightning over ocean and remote regions [N1-F1]. The evidence also implies that satellites can reduce missing events in regions where ground networks are sparse, but they may still suffer from detection efficiency tradeoffs, such as lower efficiency at night or in certain cloudy conditions [N2-F2]. In short, satellites improve coverage and detection over broad regions, while ground-based systems remain better at detailed, localized lightning detection [N3-F3][N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 4) Practical implications for monitoring and operations

Better coverage and detection support weather forecasting and hazard monitoring in several practical ways. First, GLM can detect lightning continuously over large areas and over oceans, which is especially valuable for severe weather forecasting because lightning activity can indicate intensifying thunderstorms before radar detects signs of severe weather [N1-F1]. It can also help produce earlier severe thunderstorm and tornado warnings and reduce false alarms when combined with radar, satellite data, and surface observations [N1-F1]. The evidence emphasizes that lightning is especially useful for detecting, analyzing, and forecasting severe weather, and that it can warn forecasters about possible tornadoes, large hail, damaging winds, and hurricane intensification [N1-F1]. For hazard monitoring, GLM supports lightning hazard warnings, wildfire response, aviation safety, and maritime safety, because lightning can strike far from thunderstorms and is hazardous on the water or in open areas where shelter is limited [N1-F1]. It also helps identify lightning flashes most likely to ignite wildfires, which is important for emergency response and fire mitigation [N1-F1].

Operational constraints still limit satellite lightning systems. One major constraint is the need for **cloud shielding**: the evidence says that lightning is detected from space due to the illumination of the surrounding clouds, implying that clouds can obscure lightning flashes and reduce detection [N3-R1]. GLM’s detection efficiency is also affected by orbital geometry and sensor limitations, as LIS improved detection efficiency and spatial resolution by lowering its orbit, while GLM’s geostationary vantage point gives broad coverage but not the same fine-scale resolution [N1-R3][N2-F2][N1-F1]. The evidence also indicates that satellite systems can miss lightning flashes when ground networks are sparse, and that algorithmic and data-processing challenges remain in reducing missing events and noise [N2-F2][N4-F4]. In short, satellites are powerful for large-area monitoring, but they still struggle with cloud shielding, lower resolution in some conditions, and the need for complementary ground networks to fill gaps.

Remaining gaps in spatial and temporal coverage include regions with limited radar coverage and areas where lightning activity is most intense or where ground networks are sparse. The GLM overview explicitly states that it is especially beneficial in rural or mountainous areas and over open oceans where radar and surface observations may be limited [N1-F1]. LIS is also noted as improving coverage in remote oceanic areas [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also shows that satellite systems still depend on orbital revisit times and sensor geometry to capture lightning: LIS has a 4-day revisit time, while GLM has continuous coverage but not unlimited spatial detail [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The case-study evidence implies that regional coverage has improved in some places, but gaps still exist because lightning monitoring remains uneven, especially in areas where ground networks are not dense enough [N5-R5]. Overall, better coverage and detection improve forecasting and hazard monitoring, but satellites still need to be supplemented by ground systems and improved algorithms to reduce missing events and cloud-related errors [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

### Conclusion

Overall, satellite-based lightning sensors have improved lightning monitoring over time by expanding spatial coverage from early low-Earth-orbiting sensors to continuous global monitoring via geostationary systems, while improving detection capability through better sensor design, more accurate algorithms, and improved data processing [N1-R3][N1-R1][N2-F2][N2-R5][N4-F4][N6-R1]. Satellite systems now provide broad, continuous coverage over oceans and remote areas where ground networks are sparse, but they still face tradeoffs with resolution, cloud shielding, and the need for complementary ground-based observations [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R1]. Ground-based systems remain superior for high-resolution, three-dimensional lightning characterization and detailed storm analysis, while satellites excel at large-area monitoring and early warning [N3-F3][N1-F1]. The result is a more complete, timely, and operationally useful lightning monitoring system that supports weather forecasting, hazard monitoring, and safety decision-making [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R5].
